a151.speaker: Ronald Lamola, South African International Relations Minister
a151.speech: Closing the debate, starts with a quote from Kwame Nkrumah to explain SA’s foreign policy: “We face neither East nor West; we face forward” ; quotes from a UB40 song: “We’ll fight for the right to be free. We will build our own society, and in our own society we will sing, sing our own song (Amandla Awethu, Awethu).”

a151.speaker: Ronald Lamola, South African International Relations Minister
a151.speech: “We must be self-sufficient to safeguard our continent’s future, but in the spirit of progressive internationalism, we will engage all, including the country that will succeed us as G20 President, the United States of America… Not only at home but also in terms of enhancing global health security” ; extols self-reliance: “Covid-19 taught us that we must become self-reliant or face being at the mercy of rich nations in the West who proved themselves capable of acts like hoarding lifesaving vaccines and giving us Africans the leftovers.”

a151.speaker: Ronald Lamola, South African International Relations Minister
a151.speech: Says all countries have now adopted SA’s stance that all parties must return to the table in the Russia/Ukraine conflict.

a151.speaker: Ronald Lamola, South African International Relations Minister
a151.speech: “A growing body of evidence indicates that the actions of the current US administration can be understood through what has been referred to as Project 2025.”

a151.speaker: Ronald Lamola, South African International Relations Minister
a151.speech: “Our worldview is, therefore, universal and not narrow,” saying we are concerned with the well-being of others as our well-being is linked to theirs ; notes the strong trade between SA and the US, saying it is a mutually beneficial relationship.

a151.speaker: Ronald Lamola, South African International Relations Minister
a151.speech: “We are in the business of diplomacy and dialogue. But this should never be viewed as timidity and weakness. We will continue to remain firm in this regard, hence our president’s mantra that we will not be bullied.”

a151.speaker: Ronald Lamola, South African International Relations Minister
a151.speech: Says the GNU does not supersede the Constitution and no party can represent the national interest abroad; says AfriForum and Solidarity “positioned themselves against the people of South Africa”.

a151.speaker: Project 2025 (document)
a151.speech: Extract on USAID: “US foreign aid has been transformed into a massive and open-ended global entitlement program captured by — and enriching — the progressive Left. The next conservative Administration should scale back USAID’s global footprint by, at minimum, returning to the agency’s 2019 pre–COVID–19 pandemic budget level. It should deradicalise USAID’s programs and structures and build on the conservative reforms instituted by the Trump Administration.”

a151.speaker: Emma Powell, DA MP
a151.speech: Says she is a proud South African, and we must never allow ourselves to be divided; says the sudden termination of Pepfar sent shockwaves throughout the world; says they are deeply grateful to the former US administrations for their help in the fight against HIV/Aids and that it is difficult to understand how the administration can give refugee status to one group but cut off aid ; says the GNU presents a historic opportunity for a reset: “As proud South Africans, we must recognise that unity of our nation is fundamental to this debate” ; says SA must lead from the front and calls on the US to recognise the strategic importance of maintaining strong ties with the global community of democracies.

a151.speaker: Andisiwe Kumbaca, ANC MP
a151.speech: Says it is obvious Trump’s decision was based on misinformation from the “racist” group, AfriForum; claims they are the non-political wing of the DA and FF Plus; notes the DA also went on a “bogus” trip to the US; says foreign policy is concentrated in the presidency ; says Brics in particular provides an alternative to traditional western institutions ; “The halt in US aid is not a setback”, adding it is an opportunity for greater independence: “We will not be bullied, and we will continue with the good work.”

a151.speaker: Julius Malema, EFF leader
a151.speech: Starts by referring to former US president George Bush’s “war on terror” and the disinformation campaign about weapons of mass destruction to invade Iraq; says Cuba has seen decades of sanctions and Libya has been destroyed because Gadhafi rejected US imperialism ; says the US aggression to SA is “Israel’s revenge for our moral stance” on Gaza ; “This is the early stage of economic isolation”, adding it will eventually lead to military action, and says government should dismiss right-wing groups; says the aggression doesn’t come from “fraudulent boers spreading disinformation”, but the US’ imperialism ; “The USA knows exactly what it is doing, and why it is doing it”; rejects the notion that the US has been misinformed: “The USA is the greatest perpetrator of disinformation”; “We are being punished for supporting Palestine against apartheid Israel” ; says the US will become increasingly isolated: “The world must move forward without the USA if true progress is to be achieved” and, echoing Ramaphosa, “we will not be bullied by the USA” ; says SA should stand with Russia and China ; “We are not grabbing any land, but claiming what is rightfully ours” and says they are not perpetrating a “white genocide”.

a151.speaker: Julius Malema, EFF leader
a151.speech: Speaking a second time, says Trump wanted to punish SA for its stance on Palestine: “The farmers, themselves, kill each other for greedy reasons. We cannot be told that there are farm murders in South Africa when the farmers kill the farmworkers. It is a complete lie that white people are killed in South Africa” ; says you can’t say the US is misinformed, they have the best intelligence, and they are using AfriForum as a scapegoat; says the aid wasn’t meant to help South Africa, but to control SA ; “We will never accept help that says we must perpetuate white privilege”; says America didn’t help South Africa during apartheid: “America will never choose friends for us.”

a151.speaker: Annelie Lotriet, Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly
a151.speech: Allows a moment for silent prayer or meditation, then announces the debate as the first item on the order paper and calls Malema to the podium; later asks the House to keep the volume down so that Douglas can be heard, calls on everyone to be quiet and issues Mantashe a last warning.

a151.speaker: Wesley Douglas, MKP MP
a151.speech: Says Trump’s decision is not just an economic decision, but an “act of economic coercion” and “unethical economic blackmail”; says MKP and his party leader Jacob Zuma are not anti-American and that MKP is non-aligned; says the crisis is not happening in isolation but is the direct result of “treasonous” actions by people who are harming their own country; says AfriForum and Solidarity represent a small, racist minority trying to hold onto stolen land; calls on the US to reinstall Pepfar, or phase it out, and calls on the US to respect SA’s sovereignty.

a151.speaker: Tandi Mahambehlala, Deputy Minister
a151.speech: Interrupts Douglas, asking if he wants to answer a question. He does not.

a151.speaker: Aaron Motsoaledi, South African Health Minister
a151.speech: Says he assumes most of the response to the US’ decision is expected from him, as the Health Minister; says SA has 7.8 million infected with HIV and 5.5 million are on antiretrovirals; said about 15 000 people were paid from Pepfar funds through a myriad of NGOs — “These are the person of concern in this saga” — and that 150 NGOs depend on Pepfar ; says government buys 90% of the required ARVs, the remaining is bought by a global fund, and Pepfar only funds salaries and operational costs ; “We shall not falter, come Trump or high water” about SA’s fight against HIV/Aids ; says they have met many funders, including the Solidarity Fund — “Not the Solidarity that ran to Trump, but the Solidarity Fund established during Covid” ; “Trump doesn’t owe South Africa any cent”, saying SA must stand on its own ; says he hopes they didn’t call the session to bash Trump, because it will not help.

a151.speaker: Karl le Roux, DA MP
a151.speech: Says after former US president George Bush signed Pepfar in 2003, the situation in SA with HIV/Aids improved markedly; says Pepfar is perhaps the most effective foreign aid programme; says the abrupt manner Pepfar has been stopped is unethical and that it shows SA must be more self-reliant; commends the Health Department for their response but urges the department to undergo a spending review.

a151.speaker: Mzwanele Manyi, MKP chief whip
a151.speech: Interrupts Le Roux while he speaks about his time as a medical doctor.

a151.speaker: Gwede Mantashe, Minister
a151.speech: Taunts an MKP MP who raised a point of order about their speakers being howled at: “We can’t hear you, we can’t hear you”; interrupts again unrecognised.

a151.speaker: Gijimani Skosana, ANC MP
a151.speech: Complains that they were called “howlers”.

a151.speaker: Mkhuleko Hlengwa, Deputy Transport Minister (IFP)
a151.speech: Says the geo-political landscape is changing fast; says South Africa must exercise its own sovereignty and is concerned about the 15 000 health care workers who could lose their jobs; says the IFP supports engagements based on a well-reasoned diplomatic approach and that the crisis exposes the deeper problems in the country; says some of those who benefited from apartheid never stopped working against a democratic South Africa; says the return of Trump has emboldened “these forces” — AfriForum and Solidarity; says land reform must be done responsibly and that the IFP opposes the Expropriation Act because it is flawed and risks driving SA into economic hardship, supporting transformation but not like that; says it is only the MKP that congratulated Trump on his re-election: “The chickens have come home to roost.”

a151.speaker: Gayton McKenzie, Sports, Arts and Culture Minister and PA leader
a151.speech: “America needs South Africa. South Africa needs America”; says if they don’t work together, both will lose, but SA will lose more; says South Africa must be calm and rebuild the relationship, noting Russia jumped at the chance to rebuild its relationship with the US; wants to stop giving foreign nationals medical help: “Illegal foreigners must be banned from all our hospitals, starting today. Salute.”

a151.speaker: Corne Mulder, FF Plus leader
a151.speech: Thanks Malema for bringing the topic to the House, but was concerned that Malema’s speech didn’t address the affected South Africans and was instead an attack on America; says he is concerned that there is a much bigger threat than Pepfar as the US is SA’s second biggest trading partner; says it is not true that South Africa’s relations with the US soured since Trump became president — it started under the Biden administration; says the problem is that the US considers Russia, China, Iran and North Korea as their biggest threat and SA should be aware of this, and that SA should emulate India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

a151.speaker: Athol Trollip, ActionSA parliamentary leader
a151.speech: Quoting Churchill, says the ANC has systematically chosen dishonour in their international relations and are now feeling the effects; says former International Relations Minister Naledi Pandor did everything in her power to infuriate the US; “Who the hell do AfriForum, Solidariteit and the DA think they are?” referring to their trips to the US; “Where are the real SA envoys?”; says Iran (who met with the ANC this week) and our Brics partners didn’t offer to help and that SA must stop its so-called non-aligned stance and pick a side.

a151.speaker: Kenneth Meshoe, ACDP leader
a151.speech: Says Trump’s decision was based on misinformation, as the Expropriation Act does not single out Afrikaners; says his party urges government to engage in talks with the US administration; says Ramaphosa must condemn the slaughter of Christians, especially on the African continent.

a151.speaker: Nqabayomzi Kwankwa, UDM MP
a151.speech: Says we must distinguish between the American people and a group of racists; says it was Republican George Bush who delivered Pepfar and Democrat Bill Clinton who teamed with Republicans to create Agoa, and that back then the relationship with the US was based on mutual respect; says whatever we do we must not allow ourselves to be bullied, as Ramaphosa said during SONA; is concerned that SA still depended on Pepfar years after it was instituted.

a151.speaker: Songezo Zibi, Rise Mzansi leader
a151.speech: Says we are witnessing the emergence of a dictatorship that wants to destroy democracy and they want to do it here too; echoing Ramaphosa, “We must never allow ourselves to be bullied”; says SA must understand the moment; says we face the same threat as our trading partners, a group of fascists running the US; says paid influencers are working with the fascists in South Africa and our legal framework is not equipped to deal with this disinformation.

a151.speaker: Nobuntu Hlazo-Webster, BOSA
a151.speech: Says there is a shift in the global order and those who have long dominated globally are scrambling to reassert their dominance; says Trump’s decision reflects an agenda to keep an outdated global hierarchy; says our trade relationship with the US can’t be understated but our sovereignty must be protected and it is government’s responsibility to protect its citizens; “We must take ownership of our own future… It’s time to build a South Africa that stands firm.”

a151.speaker: Vuyolwethu Zungula, ATM leader
a151.speech: Says we are a sovereign country and this must mean complete independence; says we should never allow those who give us aid to undermine our sovereignty and that other countries can’t dictate how we should deal with our problems: “Why are we even needing aid, yet we are rich in mineral resources?”; says South Africa must be prepared for potential trade actions by Trump as they could have significant implications for the African continent; says if the country was serious, AfriForum and Solidarity would have been charged with treason long ago.

a151.speaker: Alexandra Abrahams, DA MP
a151.speech: Says the withdrawal of aid calls for unity among South Africans and that SA now faces the rapid dismantling of progress in health care; “For many South Africans, this is not about politics; it is about survival”; says it is not anyone in the dome who will suffer from the withdrawal of the aid, but vulnerable people; “Where will we find billions of rands to fill the gap?”, adding they must stop spending on vanity projects such as the R28 million for advertising the NHI, and says the DA made good proposals for the budget.

a151.speaker: Thokozile Sokanyile, ANC MP
a151.speech: Says South Africa has made great strides in health care and that the NHI will be the “next great step forward” in transforming our health care; says SA is open to speak with all nations that respect our sovereignty: “We continue to speak up for a multipolar world”; says the aid withdrawal may be seen as a crisis by some, “But a crisis is also an opportunity”; “As a nation, we cannot depend on others to define ourselves.”

a151.speaker: Shameemah Salie, Al Jamah-ah MP
a151.speech: Notes Ramaphosa said South Africa will not be bullied; says SA should end its reliance on countries on the wrong side of history: “Being dependent compels us to agree to decisions that will place us on the wrong side of history”; says health care is a fundamental right and we can’t allow South Africans’ lives to be endangered; says SA must take to task entities like AfriForum and people who have served in the Israel Defence Force and who have committed genocide in Gaza.

a151.speaker: Fadiel Adams, National Coloured Congress (NCC) leader
a151.speech: Says he cannot believe South Africa allowed a convicted sexual predator to speak to us this way and that SA is not an American colony; “Does he [Trump] pay us so that Steenhuisen can live on my land?”; says AfriForum can’t be charged with treason: “It is impossible to charge a joke with treason.”

a151.speaker: John Steenhuisen, DA leader
a151.speech: Objects to Adams’ remark and says if it is the case, then Adams isn’t entitled to any land because he doesn’t own any land.

a151.speaker: Cedric Frolick, House chairperson
a151.speech: Says it is a point of debate; later says there is precedent and permits Malema to speak twice in the same debate.

a151.speaker: George Michalakis, DA chief whip
a151.speech: Asks if the same speaker may speak twice in the same debate.

a151.speaker: Mzwanele Nyhontso, Land Reform and Rural Development Minister and PAC leader
a151.speech: Says SA is under attack and we must distinguish between the attack from outside and those from within; says the US has always used lies to justify murder: “We must end all security, military and intelligence cooperation with America”; says our democracy depends on this, if we don’t want to be a victim of regime change.

a151.speaker: Wonderboy Mahlatsi, United Africans Transformation (UAT) leader
a151.speech: Says the US government’s move is another manifestation of neo-colonial oppression; says African leaders must adopt a unified approach to resource management; says the Trump administration’s decision should be a wake-up call for the whole continent.

a151.speaker: US government / USAID (termination letters)
a151.speech: Pepfar-funded HIV organisations in South Africa woke up to letters sent overnight telling them their grants have been ended — permanently; the letters stated their awards were not aligned with American national interests and they should “immediately cease all activities”.

a151.speaker: LifeLine social worker (anonymous)
a151.speech: Told News24 she felt as though she was having a panic attack on Thursday when she received the news the grants had been permanently ended: “My heart is broken”; with unpaid salaries since February and no immediate prospects, she was completing Unemployment Insurance Fund forms when News24 contacted her.

a151.speaker: The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria
a151.speech: Says it will fund the rollout of the twice-yearly anti-HIV jab, lenacapavir, for poorer countries, including South Africa, with or without the help of the US government’s AIDS fund, Pepfar.

a151.speaker: Peter Sands, Global Fund executive director
a151.speech: Told Bhekisisa: “We are still maintaining our ambition on lenacapavir for PrEP” ; “We see lenacapavir as a potential game changer in the fight against HIV as an injectable, long-acting PrEP solution that is pretty well 100% effective. It’s not going to be right for everybody, but we need to find out more from having people use it.”

a151.speaker: Professor Salim Abdool Karim, epidemiologist and director of the Centre for the Aids Programme of Research in SA (Caprisa)
a151.speech: In an exclusive interview with News24, maps the effects of Trump’s immediate withdrawal of USAID funding for South Africa’s HIV/Aids response; said the Trump administration’s sudden withdrawal was unprecedented but not surprising after a 20 January executive order froze almost all USAID funds around the world pending review; says he has been involved in many studies closed down by funders for various reasons, each of which followed a procedure to smooth the detransition — first and foremost, the funder gives a warning.

a151.speaker: Liesl Louw-Vaudran, International Crisis Group senior advisor at the African Union
a151.speech: Said the United States’ posture of putting its interests first and throwing diplomacy out the window shows that President Donald Trump has upended all sorts of established international relations practices, and that Trump’s “deal-making” style had changed the geopolitical landscape dramatically.

a151.speaker: Thani Mohamed-Soilihi, French Deputy Foreign Minister (minister delegate for Francophonie and International Partnerships)
a151.speech: Has said France and Europe will try to fill the gap left by the Trump administration’s gutting of USAID; speaking to journalists through a translator on the sidelines of the Finance in Common Summit in Cape Town, said the international situation was grave in terms of solidarity.

a151.speaker: GroundUp (report)
a151.speech: Reports that South Africa’s public health system is in turmoil after the widespread cancellation of USAID funding agreements; among others, a USAID-funded project that helped keep orphaned children on their HIV medication was forced to close, and HIV testing services are also severely impacted in some areas.

a151.speaker: Western Cape government
a151.speech: Has warned that US foreign aid funding cuts may increase the number of HIV/AIDS infections and place more pressure on the province’s health system, after the Provincial Council on AIDS and TB convened to assess the impact of the sudden termination of USAID funding to several NGOs in the Western Cape.

a151.speaker: Alan Winde, Western Cape Premier
a151.speech: Chairing the meeting, acknowledged the immediate and significant consequences of the funding halt on NGO partners: “Our NGO partners play a critical role in supporting our government’s response in tackling TB and HIV/AIDS in the Western Cape and South Africa. This abrupt termination of funding has severely disrupted essential services and left many vulnerable residents at risk. This move by the US government is heartbreaking and deeply unfortunate.”

a182.speaker: Hanan Balkhy, WHO Regional Director for the Eastern Mediterranean
a182.speech: "This crisis is tearing Sudan's health system apart. Hospitals have run out of supplies; health workers are under threat and disease is spreading in areas we can barely reach. The rainy season will multiply the health risks while further restricting access to those in need. We need urgent access and funding to provide essential care to millions of vulnerable people."

a182.speaker: Dr Hanan Balkhy, WHO Regional Director for the Eastern Mediterranean
a182.speech: "Sudan's brave health workers are achieving the impossible with almost nothing. They need protection, safe access and the tools to save lives. Time is running out."

a182.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO)
a182.speech: Since April 2023, WHO has verified 156 attacks on health care, which have killed 318 people and injured 273.

a182.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO)
a182.speech: WHO urgently calls on all parties to the conflict in Sudan to ensure unimpeded, sustained humanitarian access and to respect international humanitarian law.

a182.speaker: Famine projections / food security assessment cited
a182.speech: Famine has been confirmed in at least five areas, and projections indicate expansion in 17 areas with 24.6 million people - half the population - expected to face high levels of acute food insecurity in 2025, including 770,000 children under five estimated to suffer from severe acute malnutrition.

a238.speaker: UNICEF
a238.speech: Has expressed grave concerns about proposed reductions in international aid funding, warning that these cuts could severely impact its ability to provide essential support to millions of vulnerable children worldwide ; highlighted the alarming trend of declining contributions for the second consecutive year, emphasizing that these cuts come at a time when children's needs are greater than ever ; warns that this funding crisis could jeopardize past achievements and endanger millions more children ; urges donors to maintain their support for vital programs, emphasizing the critical need to continue assisting these vulnerable children.

a238.speaker: Catherine Russell, UNICEF Executive Director
a238.speech: "These reductions will significantly impede our capacity to reach millions of vulnerable children who depend on us for healthcare, vaccines, education, and protection from conflict." ; "If these cuts continue, many children may not receive the assistance they need to survive and thrive."

a283.speaker: Liberian People's Party (LPP), letter of 4 November 2024 signed by Chairman J. Yanqui Zaza
a283.speech: Tendered a strong letter to the Chief Executive Officer of the Liberia Electricity Corporation, Monie R. Captan, requesting that LEC publish its audited financial statements of 2015 to 2023 along with schedules of breakdown of the expenditure of the monies it received from Liberia's development partners, grounding the request in Section 1.1.12 of the 2010 Freedom of Information Act, thereby providing information on Government's subsidies allocated in the National Budget covering 2017/2018 through 2022/2023.

a283.speaker: Liberian People's Party (LPP)
a283.speech: Said Liberians will fully understand the issue of "Power Theft" at LEC more when they review the Corporation's financial statements, and that this would help compare the sad story of Power Theft versus the rosy narratives reported by the Millennium Challenge Account (MCA).

a283.speaker: Liberian People's Party (LPP)
a283.speech: Said the LEC financial statements it is demanding would explain the Agreements between LEC and the Interconnection Transmission Line running from Cote d'Ivoire, Liberia, Sierra Leone and Guinea (TRANSCO CLSG) and thereby afford the public the opportunity to see why a Section of the Agreements stipulates "...that, in the event that TRANSCO CLSG's revenues fall short of covering the project's debt service obligations, the four governments, including Liberia, will be responsible for making up revenue shortfall".

a283.speaker: Liberian People's Party (LPP)
a283.speech: Said it knows that the LEC has some information on its financial transactions included in the National Budgetary documents and on its website, but the information omitted cash balances, amount of money customers owed LEC, amount of money LEC is indebted to suppliers, and notes to the financial statements ; said it visited the LEC website 'www.lecliberia.com' and read information on Gas Pipe Contractors, Utility Cost, Electricity Prices, Electricity Suppliers and Customer Service, but not schedules and breakdowns of the USD $257M appropriated for the Corporation, nor the management fees between MCA and the Government of Liberia.

a283.speaker: Liberian People's Party (LPP)
a283.speech: "For instance, what factors affected profits/losses?" ; "Was it power theft, or other issues, including salaries, fees, etc.? Or what factors increased salary from USD $5M in 2018/19 to USD $9M in 2019/20 as detailed in the 2019/20 National Budget? Did LEC prepare a feasibility study before contracting the Ivorian electric power company to provide electricity to residents of four counties who make less than USD$5.00 per day?" ; "heartily" thanked Captan "in advance for encouraging the LEC to publish schedules of expenditures of loans and its financial statements for public consumption".

a283.speaker: Liberia Electricity Corporation official website, under Millennium Challenge Account-Liberia management
a283.speech: Reported that for the years 2015 through 2021 the LEC made a number of feats, including improving reliability of electricity supply, more than doubling the number of homes with electricity access, Mount Coffee enabling LEC to expand more reliable and affordable power supply to more than 82,000 homes, businesses and other entities compared to a little over 34,000, and the LEC becoming a viable public utility that achieved success in network reliability, availability of power-plants, collection efficiency, new customer connection, and improved customer service.

a381.speaker: National Bank of Ethiopia (latest central bank report for the second quarter of 2020/21)
a381.speech: Shows that Ethiopia's T-bill market, as usual, has been characterised by oversupply.

a381.speaker: Cepheus Capital (review)
a381.speech: According to a review carried out by Cepheus Capital a year after authorities liberalised the market, private banks and pension funds supplied the government with close to 95 billion Br in financing – with the highest yield recorded during the same period being 9.3pc for 182-day bills, reaching 10.7pc now.

a381.speaker: Patrick Heinisch, economist and capital market researcher
a381.speech: According to him, political uncertainty, domestic conflict, external pressure, sanctions and delayed debt relief may have played a role in the lack of interest. "This is particularly worrisome as the government plans to resort more frequently to the domestic market to compensate for the loss of budget support that remains suspended by major western donors," he told Fortune ; "The low yield on T-bills compared to savings deposits has made investments in T-bills unattractive," remarked Heinisch.

a381.speaker: UN-OCHA
a381.speech: According to UN-OCHA, over 854 million dollars is required to feed 5.2 million people who are in need of urgent assistance in Tigray Regional State.

a381.speaker: Ethiopian government officials
a381.speech: Criticise development partners for having “failed to keep their promises.”

a381.speaker: Observers and potential bidders
a381.speech: For observers and potential bidders, the government, which is likely to face a budget squeeze with surges in expenditure, has to offer better interest on T-bills to grab the attention of more investors.

a381.speaker: Meseret Bezabih, CEO of United Insurance
a381.speech: "We don't want to invest in T-bills as the interest is very low compared to what we get from depositing our money in banks."

a381.speaker: Asfaw Alemu, President of Dashen Bank
a381.speech: "We buy T-bills only if we have excess funds that we don't lend to our customers"; expects demand for the security would further decline as the tax season approaches, particularly during October 2021: "That is usually a time when we work under tight liquidity conditions."

a381.speaker: Abdulmenan Mohammed, financial expert
a381.speech: For him, the lack of interest for the latest T-bill auction could be seasonal. "As the yield is increasing, banks may even shift to buying T-bills at the expense of customers' borrowing. This, coupled with the strong interest of the government to finance its deficit through T-bills, would further increase the yield for it," he remarked.

a381.speaker: Eyob Tekalign (PhD), State Minister for Finance
a381.speech: While defending this year's budget before parliament, affirmed the government's emphasis on T-bills, which he said is instrumental to curb the inflationary pressure caused by the increase in the money supply.

a422.speaker: Russell Dlamini, Prime Minister of Eswatini
a422.speech: Opened the event by expressing his profound pride and humility in hosting the occasion, emphasising that the launch reaffirms a collective commitment to "building a safer, resilient, and sustainable future for our region."

a422.speaker: Russell Dlamini, Prime Minister of Eswatini
a422.speech: Highlighted the urgency of addressing drought, describing it as a "silent crisis" that has historically shaped the region's development and continues to threaten livelihoods, economies, and ecosystems; recalled the devastating 2015-2016 El Niño-induced drought that left nearly half of Eswatini's population in need of humanitarian assistance, at a cost of about E3.84 billion — 19 per cent of the national budget and 7 per cent of GDP — underscoring that reactive disaster responses are "too costly, both in resources and in human suffering."

a422.speaker: Russell Dlamini, Prime Minister of Eswatini
a422.speech: Detailed the "Eswatini Water Supply and Sanitation Access Project," financed through a World Bank loan, which improved water access in the drought-prone Shiselweni region, and reported that most project deliverables have been achieved or are nearing completion, including water infrastructure, risk profiles, municipal drought management plans and the Composite Drought Index – Eswatini (CDI-E); said the National Drought Policy ensures that "planning, budgeting and implementation across sectors are informed by risk and sustainable efforts."

a422.speaker: Russell Dlamini, Prime Minister of Eswatini
a422.speech: Cited the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015–2030), the 2015 Paris Agreement's call to limit global warming while supporting climate adaptation, and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals; said Eswatini aligns with the SADC Disaster Risk Management Strategy and Action Plan 2022, recognising that "only through collective action can we address the shared risks that transcend our borders."

a422.speaker: Russell Dlamini, Prime Minister of Eswatini
a422.speech: Said the SADC Regional Platform and the Eswatini National Platform will facilitate "dialogue, coordination, and joint action," bringing together governments, communities, civil society, the private sector, academia, and development partners to co-create solutions that are "regional in scope but speaking to local realities."

a422.speaker: Russell Dlamini, Prime Minister of Eswatini
a422.speech: Urged the University of Eswatini, the World Bank, and the SADC Secretariat to collaborate closely with the National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA) to operationalise the Eswatini Drought Centre of Excellence for the benefit of the entire African continent; praised the World Bank Group for helping Eswatini shift its perspective on drought from a mere disaster response issue to a broader development initiative, and expressed pride in the NDMA's central role in resilience building.

a422.speaker: Russell Dlamini, Prime Minister of Eswatini
a422.speech: Painted a vision of a future where communities "anticipate risks and respond early and appropriately," where regional solidarity is a "lived reality," and where innovation in risk financing, social protection and water management empowers people to "withstand shocks and continue to thrive in the face of multiple hazards"; called on participants to make the gathering a defining moment: "Let it be said that in Ezulwini, the 'Valley of Heaven,' in the Kingdom of Eswatini, we chose to strengthen our resolve, reinforced our partnerships, and raised our ambition." ; concluded with an African proverb: "When the roots are deep, there is no reason to fear the wind."

a422.speaker: Nkwe Programme of Action 2024–2029 (Eswatini national strategy document)
a422.speech: Objective 4 aims to "improve food sovereignty and sustainable development by the year 2029."

a488.speaker: Lieutenant-Colonel Omar Youssouf Omar, director of the Idriss Farah Abaneh Police Academy (APIFA)
a488.speech: In his word of welcome, described the Police Academy from the outset as a regional centre of excellence in training.

a488.speaker: Lieutenant-Colonel Omar Youssouf Omar, director of the Idriss Farah Abaneh Police Academy (APIFA)
a488.speech: "The National Police welcomes the signing of this memorandum of understanding between the Director of the National Police and the Director of the EASF, which is a force bringing together 10 countries. It is a great opportunity for the Police Academy, which will henceforth be able to host the 10 countries of this force to follow training there. It is a great pride for our country but also for the National Police."

a488.speaker: Brigadier Paul Kahuria Njema, Director of the Eastern Africa Standby Force (EASF)
a488.speech: Welcomed the launch of this training for the benefit of EASF member countries; thanked the Republic of Djibouti for having allowed the EASF to organise this important course; declared that gender representation played a key role in this kind of training and that it was crucial to strengthen women's presence.

a488.speaker: Said Nouh Hassan, Minister of the Interior of Djibouti
a488.speech: "It is an honour for me to speak at the ceremony launching the training on child protection held under the sponsorship of the Eastern Africa Standby Force. As you know, the issue of child protection is a crucial challenge for our country but also for the whole world and above all for the African continent. More than 60% of inhabitants are under 30 years old and more than 200 million children are in the 15 to 24 age bracket. It is therefore our duty to watch over their well-being and their safety in order to make them responsible adults concerned about the future of their continent. The objective of this training is to allow participants to immerse themselves in themes relating to child protection in order to prevent together the risks they may face in a world beset by incessant conflicts."

a488.speaker: Colonel Mohamed Aden Barkhad, administrative and financial director of the EASF
a488.speech: "We signed today a memorandum of understanding with a view to allowing the Police Academy to become a training centre for the EASF. As you know, the EASF is a mechanism bringing together 10 countries. Djibouti plays an important role within this force. I would also like to recall that the academy has already hosted other training of this kind, but the particularity today is the signing of this memorandum of understanding which will henceforth allow APIFA to establish itself even more as a regional training centre."

a488.speaker: Langmo Johnny, Police Adviser of the EASF
a488.speech: "I would like to thank all the member states of this force for their presence here. Child protection plays an important role in peacekeeping. Children are the first victims in the event of conflict and instability, as are their families. The world faces several challenges and today more than yesterday it is important to concentrate our efforts on better cooperation. I would like in this regard to remind the participating countries to show diligence during this training on child protection."

a598.speaker: Diina Nashidengo, Director of Trade, Namibian Ministry of Industry, Mines and Energy
a598.speech: In her closing remarks stressed that the week-long training had demanded "focus, teamwork and commitment", and that participants were going home "not only with new skills and knowledge, but also with stronger networks across Africa" ; emphasised that the course had strengthened solidarity among African States Parties and called on participants to pass on their knowledge as ambassadors of the OPCW and to promote operational readiness in their home countries ; called on participants to "keep working for a safer Africa and a safer world".

a598.speaker: Diina Nashidengo, Director of Trade, Namibian Ministry of Industry, Mines and Energy
a598.speech: Underlined Namibia's pride in co-hosting the programme with the OPCW, saying that hosting it repeatedly showed the confidence placed in the country to strengthen African capacities under the Chemical Weapons Convention.

a598.speaker: Babatunde Olowookere, OPCW programme officer
a598.speech: Explained that the training had strengthened participants' practical skills in dealing with chemical incidents, and called on them to pass this knowledge on within their institutions in order to promote national capacity-building.

a598.speaker: OPCW (Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons)
a598.speech: Had confirmed in 2023 that all declared chemical weapons stockpiles had been destroyed, but at the same time warned against complacency.

a772.speaker: Public Citizen, citizens’ rights advocacy group
a772.speech: Appealed to a federal court in Washington to put an end to what it calls the “illegal, systematic and ongoing disclosures of personal and financial information” by Elon Musk or other members of the “Department of Government Efficiency” (Doge).

a772.speaker: Wired (website)
a772.speech: According to the website Wired, the boss of Tesla, X and SpaceX has placed young people working for Doge in key government positions, and these teams now have unprecedented access to the payments system, normally the preserve of apolitical senior civil servants.

a772.speaker: Elizabeth Warren, Democratic Senator and member of the Senate Banking Committee
a772.speech: Described the situation as “extremely dangerous” in a letter to Scott Bessent.

a772.speaker: Ron Wyden, Senator representing Oregon
a772.speech: Explained that Elon Musk represented a national security risk, because of his unlimited access to certain financial data.

a772.speaker: Federal government employees’ union
a772.speech: Also sounded the alarm in order to recall the laws in force, which normally require safeguards.

a772.speaker: Tim Waltz, former running mate of Kamala Harris
a772.speech: Criticised the billionaire who appears to be taking on considerable weight in the American administration: “Elon Musk is a terrible president,” he wrote.

a772.speaker: Elon Musk (posts on X)
a772.speech: For several weeks he has been multiplying his provocations on his social network X, notably calling for a vote for the German far-right party AfD and sharply criticising the British Prime Minister.

a954.speaker: Gilles Ganivet, cooperation and cultural action counsellor of the Embassy of France in Burundi
a954.speech: “A first fair – I repeat it, and I am very happy and proud – a first fair organised in Burundi,” he exclaimed during a press conference on 25 April; according to him, this first fair will be held on Tuesday 2 May 2023, with an institutional session in the morning from 9 a.m. bringing together French and Burundian higher education institutions at the French Institute of Burundi, and the fair open to students at the French School of Bujumbura in the afternoon at 1:30 p.m. and the following day, Wednesday 3 May 2023, from 9 a.m.

a954.speaker: Perrine Chuker, head of Campus France
a954.speech: “Different French higher education institutions will be here in Bujumbura from 1 to 4 May to meet Burundian higher education institutions. The idea is to be able to forge future partnerships between these various institutions.” ; She explains that students will meet the French higher education institutions at their stands: “Students will be able to move freely between the stands and will be able to meet around ten French higher education institutions that will be present at the French School of Bujumbura.” ; “Entry will be free. The exact programme as well as all the schools that will be present will be announced on the website of Campus France Burundi and on social media.”

a954.speaker: The organisers
a954.speech: According to the organisers, students' choice is driven by academic and research excellence, the low cost of higher education and the variety of its higher education offer.

a1067.speaker: Saara Kuugongelwa-Amadhila, Prime Minister of Namibia
a1067.speech: Expressed concern over reported incidents of theft of drought-relief food items: "Government has noted with concern the reported incidents of theft of drought-relief food items. We also condemn the reported politicising of emergency food assistance. These incidents must be addressed by all stakeholders within the applicable policies and systems" ; "We will not be able to effectively address the vulnerabilities created by the drought if we allow such incidents to continue as they undermine efforts to ensure assistance [is provided] to all those in need."

a1067.speaker: Nangolo Mbumba, President of Namibia
a1067.speech: In May declared a national state of emergency due to the drought, the official declaration published on 22 May in the Government Gazette; in his address to the Southern African Development Community (SADC) summit he discussed the severe impacts of the El Nino-induced drought and floods across member states and revealed that Namibia's drought-relief programme faces a funding shortfall of N$482 million, calling for assistance from international and regional stakeholders.

a1067.speaker: Namibian Sun (earlier report)
a1067.speech: Reported earlier this month on the tragic deaths of about 20 people in the Judea Lyaboloma constituency of the Zambezi Region, residents who were forced to fetch water from dangerous areas where they risked encounters with crocodiles and hippos.

a1067.speaker: Richard Mukube, Mashi conservancy manager
a1067.speech: Confirmed that a lack of access to potable water is forcing people into these dangerous areas.

a1067.speaker: Namibian environment ministry
a1067.speech: Reported on Tuesday that more than 130 hippos are stranded in the muddy Munambeza Pond near Lake Lyambezi in Zambezi, trapped due to dwindling water levels, with five already dead - the third site along the Chobe River where hippos have become stranded.

a1067.speaker: Romeo Muyunda, spokesperson of the environment ministry (to NBC)
a1067.speech: Told NBC that efforts are underway to improve the situation for the stranded animals: "We have drilled boreholes, and we are already pumping water into the ponds. While the situation is dire, we believe it can be salvaged."

a1067.speaker: Randy Berry, United States ambassador to Namibia
a1067.speech: Announced in July that the United States - through the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) - will provide US$5 million (approximately N$90 million) in humanitarian aid to support drought-affected populations in Namibia.

a1098.speaker: Bola Tinubu, Nigerian President
a1098.speech: Pleaded with his compatriots for "patience" as they continue to grapple with a tough economic situation; in an independence day speech defended his controversial economic reforms, saying they were necessary and are beginning to bear results ; "I am deeply aware of the struggles many of you face in these challenging times… I plead for your patience as the reforms we are implementing show positive signs, and we are beginning to see light at the end of the tunnel." ; said his administration had no choice but to put the economy on a more sustainable path, and noted that numerous other countries across the world have seen an increased cost of living.

a1098.speaker: Bola Tinubu, Nigerian President
a1098.speech: Insisted Nigeria is "winning the war" on the violence that has killed thousands in the north over recent years ; "I am happy to announce to you, my compatriots, that our administration is winning the war on terror and banditry." ; added that the government has eliminated commanders from Boko Haram "faster than ever".

a1098.speaker: Michael Olaleye, Lagos resident
a1098.speech: Told the Reuters news agency: "Personally, me I am doubting if it is something that is going to work out because it has not shown really… majority of what the president is talking about has not shown."

a1098.speaker: Victory Azimih, Lagos city dweller
a1098.speech: Urged Nigerians to be "optimistic" and acknowledge that the government cannot "fix everything".

a1098.speaker: Nigerian military spokesperson
a1098.speech: Said earlier this week that troops "neutralised" almost 2,000 "terrorists" in the third quarter of the year.

a1098.speaker: Local residents in Kaduna state
a1098.speech: According to local residents, a military airstrike that targeted armed gangs in Kaduna state last week, killing 24 people, hit a mosque and homes instead.

a1098.speaker: Local media in Nigeria
a1098.speech: Reported two days ago that armed assailants killed at least two people and kidnapped 44 others in separate attacks in the states of Zamfara and Kaduna.

a1098.speaker: Protest organisers
a1098.speech: Saying they were against "the devastation, hunger, insecurity and the hardship that this government has unleashed on Nigerians".

a1279.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a1279.speech: has said he will cut all future funding to South Africa over allegations that it was confiscating land and "treating certain classes of people very badly". On Sunday, Trump wrote on his social media platform Truth Social: "I will be cutting off all future funding to South Africa until a full investigation of this situation has been completed!" ; He later said, in a briefing with journalists, that South Africa's "leadership is doing some terrible things, horrible things". "So that's under investigation right now. We'll make a determination, and until such time as we find out what South Africa is doing — they're taking away land and confiscating land, and actually they're doing things that are perhaps far worse than that."

a1279.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, South African President (statement on X)
a1279.speech: "South Africa is a constitutional democracy that is deeply rooted in the rule of law, justice and equality. The South African government has not confiscated any land." ; Ramaphosa said that the only funding South Africa received from the US was through the health initiative Pepfar, which represented "17% of South Africa's HIV/Aids programme". ; The South African president stressed the government had not confiscated any land. The new law was not a "confiscation instrument, but a constitutionally mandated legal process that ensures public access to land in an equitable and just manner as guided by the constitution".

a1279.speaker: Elon Musk, Trump adviser (post on X)
a1279.speech: "Why do you have openly racist ownership laws?"

a1279.speaker: US government data
a1279.speech: The US allocated about $440m (£358m) in assistance to South Africa in 2023, according to US government data.

a1279.speaker: South African government spokesperson (during Trump's first term)
a1279.speech: South Africa accused Trump of seeking to sow division, with a spokesperson saying he was "misinformed".

a1386.speaker: Ambassador Stephan Auer, German Ambassador to Ethiopia
a1386.speech: On the 10 million euro agreement signed with the UNDP: "We want to encourage the peace efforts undertaken by the government of Ethiopia and the Tigray Administration. The Pretoria Agreement, signed almost a year ago, clearly demonstrates that conflicting parties have chosen the path of finding a political solution. They demonstrated that there is no military solution to the conflict. But there needs to be a political solution. We want to support this, providing resources to the UNDP Peace Support Facility." ; "We want to see the people benefit from peace, with a quick and fast peace dividend, following the political and not the military track."

a1386.speaker: Ambassador Stephan Auer, German Ambassador to Ethiopia
a1386.speech: On criticism that the intervention came too late: "Germany, the European Union (EU) and other member states always champion a political solution because we do not believe in a military solution. You can always argue that we could have come earlier. But it has come nonetheless, and that is the main thing. We have to see that the cessation of hostilities agreement is implemented fully."

a1386.speaker: Ambassador Stephan Auer, German Ambassador to Ethiopia
a1386.speech: On how diplomacy has evolved in the era of hyper-connectivity: "Diplomacy has become much more fast-paced; we have a very dynamic diplomacy. We must adapt to the new possibilities and opportunities through social media and the Internet. Consider that the fax machine was just introduced when I joined the Foreign Office in 1988." ; "There are also some disadvantages with a lot of disinformation and misinformation in social media that can be used for hate, increasing tensions between ethnicities, parties, and partners. Unfortunately, we have seen quite a lot of disinformation, mainly coming now through the Russian media, about the Russian aggression of Ukraine. We must counter this with objective information, proving it is wrong." ; "I am excited about the opportunities because they can contribute a lot to inform people about what we are doing. But at the same time, we also have to see that it is not abused. We have to strike a balance."

a1386.speaker: Ambassador Stephan Auer, German Ambassador to Ethiopia
a1386.speech: On Germany's five decades in the United Nations and its responsibilities: "In September 1973, we joined the United Nations with the second German state at that time, the German Democratic Republic (GDR)... Germany used to be considered the enemy state after the Second World War. Under the Nazi regime from 1938 to 1945, atrocities and crimes were committed on German soil. We are and will always stand up to our responsibilities... we are committed to fighting for the principles of the United Nations, particularly its Charter... defending the principles of human rights, territorial integrity, sovereignty, and peaceful resolution of conflicts. This is why we were particularly appalled by the blatant violation of these principles by the Russian attack on Ukraine to change borders violently using military means. We cannot accept it, and we have to fight." ; "We need an effective United Nations system, and we support the membership of Africa in the Security Council, where we feel it is underrepresented. We also support a better representation of Africa in the multilateral systems, and we are happy to see the African Union (AU) join the G20 as a member. We would be delighted if Africans would support the G4, where Germany, Japan, Brazil and India aspire to join the Security Council as permanent members."

a1386.speaker: Ambassador Stephan Auer, German Ambassador to Ethiopia
a1386.speech: On African countries' reluctance to condemn Russia: "As a German diplomat, it is difficult for me to say what drives African countries not to condemn this violation of the United Nations Charter and its principles. I can only say that we have an obvious and blatant violation of the principles corresponding to the principles the AU upholds: territorial integrity, sovereignty, non-interference in internal affairs, and the protection of human rights." ; "What surprises me is that many African countries are not addressing the implications of all crimes perpetrated by the Russians in Ukraine and against Ukrainian citizens. The impact of this war on their populations, such as the rise of fuel and fertiliser prices, is the consequence of the Russian aggression and the ending of the Black Sea Green Initiative by Russia."

a1386.speaker: Ambassador Stephan Auer, German Ambassador to Ethiopia
a1386.speech: On the post-World War II global order and double standards: "I would say that this world order is very much in favour of the weaker countries and states. It protects those vulnerable against those who believe 'might is right.' We need to see that this rule-based international order is maintained and protected because it defends the weaker ones. If you uphold principles, you must do it when it comes to aggression against a sovereign country, whether in Africa, America or Asia. Principles are universal..." ; "The international order may not have benefited Africa. But it helped a lot of other countries on other continents, such as South Korea, Singapore, and the Asian Tiger countries." ; asked whether the West is faithful to these principles, he replied "The question is always, 'Who's the West?'" and "I can only speak for Germany. We have principle-based policies. We do not apply double standards in our foreign policy."

a1386.speaker: Ambassador Stephan Auer, German Ambassador to Ethiopia
a1386.speech: On the Sustainable Development Goals: "I hope the SDGs adopted in 2015 will be achieved. We all know that it is midterm through 2030. I hope it will be fulfilled because 90pc of all global problems will be addressed if we do." ; "I want to highlight the SDG-16, which promotes peace, stability, justice, and the rule of law. This is the basis for development and one of the structural deficits of the previous Millennium Development Goals (MDGs). It does not make sense to build a bridge that violent conflicts on the following day would destroy."

a1386.speaker: Ambassador Stephan Auer, German Ambassador to Ethiopia
a1386.speech: On Germany's contribution to the SDGs and energy transition: "we are trying to transform our energy system and help our economy phase out fossil fuel in the medium to long term. We have ambitious climate goals... We are trying to reduce our carbon emissions by 80pc in 2040, and to be climate neutral by 2045... By 2030, we want to accomplish over 80pc of our electricity generation through renewable energies." ; "We also help other countries transform their energy systems and economies. We partner with over 30 countries worldwide, including Ethiopia, in the climate and energy sector. Ethiopia has a lot of potential for renewables - wind and solar - but also for hydrogen, produced with solar energy."

a1386.speaker: Ambassador Stephan Auer, German Ambassador to Ethiopia
a1386.speech: On leapfrogging technology and climate financing: "I am not an expert in this, but for instance, in the telecommunications sector... Today, you no longer need fixed lines; you use your mobile... Yes, you can do it [leapfrog]; but, you need to have the technology and know what and how to do it with the support of those who already have it. Hence, the importance of partners willing and able to transfer the technology. You would also need to create the legal framework to attract these investments..." ; "Here we are with the problem of climate financing. I agree that the international community has not lived up to its responsibilities and promises. I can assure you that Germany is one of the most significant contributors to climate finance."

a1386.speaker: Ambassador Stephan Auer, German Ambassador to Ethiopia
a1386.speech: On Europe's position between China and Russia in a multipolar order: "We will always uphold the principles adopted after the Second World War - striving for peace and security, human rights protection and promoting a free and open economy... a social market economy, as we call it in Germany." ; "We have China as a growing superpower, but it is a partner when it comes to the economic cooperation front. It is also an adversary or sort when it comes to the political system. We have adopted the 'China Strategy' in Germany to tackle our challenges." ; "Russia has nothing to offer besides weapons and mercenaries with which African countries can further destroy themselves. The mercenaries come to exploit the minerals and support authoritarian regimes. The problem is not only that these mercenaries cannot be controlled; they are turning against the regimes that created them..." ; "We believe that in the long run, human beings are very interested and in favour of a free and open society, not controlled by the state... We see it through many migrants who try to come to Europe and not going to China or Russia."

a1386.speaker: Ambassador Stephan Auer, German Ambassador to Ethiopia
a1386.speech: On a new cold war, European integration and Germany's dependence on Russian gas: "We, unfortunately, are already in a pretty tricky place. We see now in Europe the violation of principles we adopted after the Second World War to establish a new security order... Our answer to that is to uphold the principles and regional integration." ; "The process of political and economic integration is the way forward... Thus, we support the African Union integration process as the biggest bilateral donor to the AU." ; "We also want to integrate Russia into our economic system. We have imported a lot of Russian gas; we depended on it, thinking Russia would have the economic interest in keeping it." ; asked whether this was Merkel's miscalculation: "It was a miscarriage... I was convinced that this approach ensured peace and security in Europe after the Second World War... But there are limits to what you can do if you have a leader who thinks about power politics and does not think about his population..."

a1386.speaker: Ambassador Stephan Auer, German Ambassador to Ethiopia
a1386.speech: On how Ethiopia fits into Germany's Africa strategy: "I think nobody can be happy with what is happening in this country at the moment. We are very concerned about the conflicts going on. However, we are also encouraged at the same time by the efforts of this government to solve the problems politically... The first round of talks with OLA encourages us, too. We hope the conflicts in the Amhara region will also be resolved politically." ; "We are interested in Ethiopia as a peaceful, stable and prosperous country. With over 120 million inhabitants, Ethiopia is the political and economic powerhouse in the region... We have doubled our humanitarian assistance, helping to have the peace dividend. We are trying to foster the economy through the promotion of direct investments. Under the German G-20 presidency, we initiated the 'Compact with Africa' Initiative, where 12 African countries, including Ethiopia, are members."

a1386.speaker: Ambassador Stephan Auer, German Ambassador to Ethiopia
a1386.speech: On the UN human rights commission on Ethiopia and transitional justice: "I do not see it as a contradiction. When the Commission was established, it was right after the start of the war. We now have the Pretoria Agreement and a joint report released by the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission and the Office of the High Representative for Human Rights. This report has some recommendations, amongst other things, for establishing a transitional justice mechanism... the Ethiopian authorities expressed their commitment to establishing a credible and inclusive transitional justice mechanism." ; "We have the commitment from the government to bring the perpetrators of human rights violations to justice... It is much more critical that the government and the people bring human rights violations, war crimes, and crimes against humanity before their own courts. It is the ownership that matters... However, it does not mean that this issue cannot be addressed, again, in the Human Rights Council at a later stage if things do not develop in the way the Ethiopian government has committed to do." ; "We will see whether a transitional justice mechanism is credible and corresponds to international standards." ; "We know the concerns about the human rights situation in this country that the conflicts will not alleviate the situation and will continue exacerbating human suffering. But we need to address the root causes of the conflicts. I am encouraged by the transitional justice mechanism which will be established. The national dialogue process also equally encourages me."

a1386.speaker: Ambassador Stephan Auer, German Ambassador to Ethiopia
a1386.speech: On whether Europe has traded human rights principles for migration concerns: "I do not see this because we are still upholding human rights. A recent example is the 10 million euro support package for the Peace Support Facility, where we are not only supporting economic development and livelihoods but also social causes and the protection of human rights. We support the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission, under the fantastic leadership of Daniel Bekele, who is doing an excellent job there." ; "I do not see a trade-off between human rights and migration. The migration routes do not go from Ethiopia primarily to Europe. They go to the Arabian Peninsula first and Southern Africa. The third route goes to Europe."

a1386.speaker: Ambassador Stephan Auer, German Ambassador to Ethiopia
a1386.speech: On resuming political dialogue and the National Dialogue Commission: "Absolutely. This is why the national dialogue is so important. We think you can only solve these problems if you address the root causes... It is up to the Ethiopians to decide what should be discussed at the national dialogue. What we are doing in Germany and Europe is to support this process, offering expertise and resources." ; "The most important thing will be to see how the national dialogue will be carried out and whether it is inclusive. We heard in the beginning that several opposition parties were reluctant to participate. But more are joining now. I hope that in the country's interest, in the end, we will have all parties around the table at the national dialogue. Equally important is for civil society representatives of the different regions to come together and talk about the problems of this country."

a1386.speaker: Ambassador Stephan Auer, German Ambassador to Ethiopia
a1386.speech: On supporting non-state actors: "We work very closely with humanitarian NGOs. When it comes to human rights, we work with NGOs that defend and protect human rights. We are aware and willing to contribute to a lively civil society because we believe they contribute a lot to a vibrant political and economic order."

a1386.speaker: Ambassador Stephan Auer, German Ambassador to Ethiopia
a1386.speech: On German investment in Ethiopia and the forex crunch: "We have a lot of small and medium-sized enterprises... They are risk averse because these small and medium-sized enterprises can easily face bankruptcy if an investment goes wrong. Their advantage is that if they come, they are interested in establishing added values, creating jobs, training people and transferring technologies and expertise. They would come here to stay. But, for them to come, you need a safe environment and that there is peace and stability. It would help if you also had to protect their investments with the rule of law and fighting corruption. And this is a challenge at the moment." ; "The forex crunch is not only for companies that want to take out the profits they made, but also to refinance investments... This is why we hope the Homegrown Economic Reform 2.0 will be implemented soon. Entailing bold reforms, we hope it will address the problems of the forex crunch." ; "The energy, packaging, and agriculture sectors have massive potential in this country. If the legal and business environments improve, I can imagine that many companies would be interested in investing in Ethiopia." ; on the electric automotive industry: "It depends very much on the business environment and the potential here. We have had folks who are interested over here recently. They have shown their interest in working with Ethiopian companies to establish a training unit for mechanics and eventually establish a manufacturing assembly line."

a1386.speaker: Ambassador Stephan Auer, German Ambassador to Ethiopia
a1386.speech: On debt restructuring and reform of multilateral financial institutions: "Germany is very conscious that there is a lot of debt problem in many countries, particularly in Africa. The COVID pandemic has aggravated the situation. The G-20 countries have adopted the sustainability initiative for debts (DSSI)... Germany has always supported these, and we think the G-20 framework and the Paris Club are instrumental in alleviating the burden for the heavily indebted countries... But of course, Germany is not one of the biggest creditors, and there are limits to what we can do." ; "We are in favour of reforming the international financial architecture in a way that further helps developing developing countries. We have to address the issues African countries face. But they have to clearly define what they want. I have not seen a proposal showing what African countries want to see in reforming the international financial architecture. If we know what Africa wants, we can address it." ; "We will see what we can do. We are also interested in how Africa will be represented in the BRICS Development Bank."

a1386.speaker: Head of the UN Commission (of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia)
a1386.speech: Said the national transitional justice process is not credible because the government is to be held accountable.

a1386.speaker: Tigray provisional authorities
a1386.speech: Recently issued a statement rejecting transitional justice under the federal government and the Commission.

a1386.speaker: Ethiopian authorities
a1386.speech: In the many talks held with them and in public, expressed their commitment to establishing a credible and inclusive transitional justice mechanism; they have established a working group to work out the principles and mechanism, which will then be presented to the Cabinet.

a1902.speaker: Samuel Batcho, Coordinator of the Coordination Unit for the formulation of the 2nd programme and the monitoring of reforms of MCA-Benin (UCF)
a1902.speech: Indicated that no one is unaware of the importance, place and role of energy in the development of a nation, recalling population growth and the subsequent needs which remain a subject of great concern ; observed that many people do not have sufficient energy and that only 25% of Africans have access to modern energy.

a1902.speaker: Samuel Batcho, Coordinator of the Coordination Unit for the formulation of the 2nd programme and the monitoring of reforms of MCA-Benin (UCF)
a1902.speech: Specified that, pending the signing of the 2nd Compact in December 2015 and its implementation or operationalisation in 2016, the programme, which involves an amount of US$300 million, extends over a full five years.

a1902.speaker: Gabriel Dégbègni, Infrastructure Officer, and Grégoire Zinsou, Assistant to the Coordinator
a1902.speech: Said that only a third of Benin's population has access to electricity, that demand continues to grow rapidly and is forecast to double within the next five years, while supply sources are far from sufficient ; recalled that the challenge lies in the approach of the Beninese government, which is exploring new national sources of energy production both to supply consumers connected to the electricity grid and those who are off-grid ; went on to say that Benin's MCC Compact would help to provide solutions for the existing electricity grid as well as off-grid solutions in order to address the country's energy deficits.

a1902.speaker: Gabriel Dégbègni, Infrastructure Officer, and Grégoire Zinsou, Assistant to the Coordinator
a1902.speech: Specified that MCC and UCF wish to gather information and ideas on potential projects in the following areas of intervention: essential public infrastructure such as water treatment and pumping facilities, hospitals, clinics, universities, schools and ports; the production and distribution of electricity at community and municipal level; household-level production and storage; and energy efficiency measures ; said that potential applicants include, among others, academic institutions, industrial groups, non-profit and for-profit organisations, commercial companies, faith-based organisations and civil society organisations.

a2106.speaker: Michael Raynor, United States Ambassador to Benin
a2106.speech: Expressed his gratitude to the Beninese government and people for the good times he was able to spend during his three years of mission in Benin: "I am truly honoured to have represented my country here for three years. I had the privilege of discovering the many riches of this country and I was above all impressed by the dynamism of the women and young people of Benin" ; gave assurances that his departure would change nothing in the bilateral cooperation between the United States and Benin, cooperation which he had tried to strengthen during his stay in Cotonou.

a2106.speaker: Boni Yayi, President of the Republic of Benin
a2106.speech: Saluted "a great friend" of Benin who shares with the United States the values of the free world: "For three years, you accepted our shortcomings, you accompanied us in our reforms" ; said the Beninese people are attached to democracy, which does not go hand in hand with destitution: "We must avoid the gap between destitution and democracy. If destitution is severe, it betrays democracy. Likewise, democracy does not go with a failing education system, a shortfall in health services, or a deficit in infrastructure, primarily energy."

a2106.speaker: Boni Yayi, President of the Republic of Benin
a2106.speech: Hailed the American diplomat's involvement in securing the second Millennium Challenge Account compact, estimated at 411 million dollars: "It is the first time that a country has received an amount higher than what it had received under the first compact", and assured the United States of his government's determination to improve governance.

a2285.speaker: Scott Perry, US Congressman (Republican, Pennsylvania)
a2285.speech: Had alleged that USAID was providing funding to terrorist organisations, including Boko Haram. He said this during the inaugural hearing of the Subcommittee on Delivering on Government Efficiency last week. He said, "Your money, $697 million annually, plus the shipments of cash funds Madrasas, ISIS, Al-Qaeda, Boko Haram, ISIS Khorasan, terrorist training camps."

a2285.speaker: President Donald Trump's Department of Government Efficiency
a2285.speech: USAID has recently been put under intense scrutiny, particularly from President Donald Trump's Department of Government Efficiency, alleging that it was mismanaging and wasting U.S. taxpayer funds.

a2285.speaker: Dr. Isma'il Tanko Wudilawa, retired Joint Task Force (JTF) Commander
a2285.speech: Has responded to claims by U.S. lawmaker Scott Perry that USAID is allegedly sponsoring acts of terrorism worldwide, including in Nigeria. Speaking to DAILY POST in Kano, Dr. Wudilawa also pointed to visible signs of foreign involvement in Nigeria's security crisis, particularly in the tactics and operations of Boko Haram terrorists. He highlighted that the insurgents possess advanced military training, sophisticated weaponry, and other forms of support that could only come through external partnerships. He called on both the Nigerian government and the public to remain vigilant and patriotic.

a2411.speaker: Lazarus Chakwera, President of Malawi
a2411.speech: Expressed his appreciation to local organizations and development partners for their unwavering support and dedication in ensuring food availability to Malawians during this period of food security crisis; stressed the importance of seeking international support to address the humanitarian crisis the country is currently grappling with.

a2411.speaker: Lazarus Chakwera, President of Malawi
a2411.speech: Recognised significant contributions that Malawi has received from various development partners through the World Food Programme (WFP); said WFP will publicly disclose the details of how and where the aid has been distributed; pointed out that Malawi has received substantial financial support from governments around the world through the WFP, including 11.8 million dollars from Sweden and the Netherlands, 7 million dollars from the United States, 3.8 million dollars from the United Kingdom, 1.9 million dollars from Japan, 1.6 million dollars from France, 1.5 million dollars from South Korea, and 1.07 million dollars from Germany.

a2411.speaker: Lazarus Chakwera, President of Malawi
a2411.speech: Specifically commended partners such as Good Neighbors Malawi, Nkhoma Synod, Emerging Donor March Fund, Save the Children, UNICEF, BHA, FAO, Mary's Meals, USAID, JBJ Foundation, ISRAID, and Caritas partners for their steadfast support, and urged these partners to continue their efforts in mobilising support for Malawi from across the globe to alleviate the lives of Malawians.

a2537.speaker: Maialen Chourraut, Spanish kayaker
a2537.speech: Admitted that the arrival of Kayak Cross as an Olympic event was one reason she had kept on training with a view to Paris.

a2758.speaker: Francoise Sybille Assavedo, Deputy Director of Cabinet of the Minister of Health of Benin
a2758.speech: Recalled, opening the proceedings, that this meeting follows the one held in Abidjan, Cote d'Ivoire, in June 2023, and stressed that it serves as a framework for taking stock of the implementation of large-scale food fortification programmes in West Africa and for sharing good practices and the lessons learned in each country.

a2758.speaker: Francoise Sybille Assavedo, Deputy Director of Cabinet of the Minister of Health of Benin
a2758.speech: "Food and nutrition problems remain a brake on development in West Africa and persist because of their complex determinants, at once cultural, social and economic"; she developed that the deficiency in key micronutrients, notably iron, vitamin A, folic acid, zinc and iodine, remains at an alarming level among both children and women of childbearing age.

a2758.speaker: Dr Keita Namoudou, West African Health Organisation (WAHO/Ooas)
a2758.speech: Indicated that the workshop allows participants to carry out a SWOT analysis (strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats) of existing projects and interventions, and that the aim is to identify methodological approaches, the limits and the paths for improving public-private partnership and sub-regional governance for the sustainability of fortification efforts, in order to prevent nutrient deficiencies and improve the overall health of the populations of West Africa.

a2758.speaker: Dr William Bosu, West African Health Organisation (WAHO/Ooas)
a2758.speech: Added that one woman in two of childbearing age is anaemic, with severe deficiencies in micronutrients indispensable to the proper functioning of the organism; that one child in three under five is stunted; and that 15% of infants have a low birth weight in the region.

a2758.speaker: Lassane Kabore, representative of ECOWAS
a2758.speech: Said it is important to propose actions to be replicated and advocacy avenues for the sustainability of the fortification strategy in West Africa in order to free populations from the tyranny of hunger and poor nutrition.

a2897.speaker: Relatives and eyewitnesses (Gololey village, Bal'ad District)
a2897.speech: Told Horn Observer that the Somali national army on Wednesday executed eight young professionals in a cold blooded manner following an al-Shabaab attack in Gololey village in Bal'ad District, Middle Shabelle region.

a2897.speaker: Abdikarin Hussein Guled, Somali presidential aspirant
a2897.speech: Has called for a united front to combat against Covid-19 in Somalia as the Somalis already face social and economic effects of the pandemic.

a2897.speaker: 2020 Humanitarian Needs Overview
a2897.speech: According to the 2020 Humanitarian Needs Overview, an estimated 5.2 million people in Somalia need humanitarian assistance, including 1.7 million people who have been displaced by conflict, insecurity, forced evictions, droughts and floods.

a2948.speaker: Margarida Talapa, President of the Mozambican Assembly of the Republic
a2948.speech: Expressed the Mozambican parliament's desire to strengthen cooperation relations with the Palestinian National Council (PNC); said the Assembly of the Republic will continue to defend the independence and self-determination of the Palestinians in the international forums in which the Mozambican parliament is a full member. "To express the interest of the Assembly of the Republic in strengthening cooperation relations between the two States, in particular in the parliamentary sphere," she said.

a2948.speaker: Margarida Talapa, President of the Mozambican Assembly of the Republic
a2948.speech: Said Mozambique remains sensitive to the war in Palestine, especially with the worsening of the humanitarian situation, and has been raising support and channelling it to the Palestinians. "This involves raising money, food, hygiene products, clothing and other important items. A similar action also took place in 2023," she said, stressing that the support comes from various people and entities. ; Appeals for an immediate end to the atrocities committed against innocent people, reiterating that Mozambique is available to make its contribution as a way of ensuring the resolution of the conflict.

a2948.speaker: Aziz Dweik, President of the Palestinian National Council (letter)
a2948.speech: Letter delivered to Talapa congratulating her on her democratic and transparent election to the post of President of the Assembly of the Republic, which took place in mid-January.
